Code corpora are generally divided into two types: fixed corpora and intelligent corpora. For
fixed corpora, users preset code snippets, which are then prompted to the user by listening to
shortcut keys entered by the user to search for the corresponding snippet. This code generation
method is simple and fast, but it suffers from poor scalability and suboptimal user experience,
and developers need to know the key values and corresponding snippets in advance.
The acquisition of intelligent corpora mainly depends on the capability of the code repository
itself and the assistance of models. Typical examples include the GitHub Copilot plugin and
N-gram models. The VSCode plugin Kite Autocomplete uses the N-gram model and is trained
on over 25 million files, enhancing coding efficiency through code assistance functions during
programming. It predicts the content that the user is about to input based on context and current
input. Additionally, it can read ahead in the context of the entire file to further infer the user’s
actions based on current input. Taking code completion as an example, using a JavaScript code
corpus and applying the N-gram probability model to complete code development, the relevant
workflow is shown in Figure 9.9.

Unlike code completion, code generation (also known as code intent generation) refers to
inferring the function of code based on its content. Well-known industry open-source models
and services include code2vec and code2seq. The advantage of code2vec lies in code functionality
summarization, whereas code2seq excels at code functionality description.

Instead of starting from existing code snippets, functional-description-based methods begin
with natural language descriptions of what the program should do.
Code generation and completion based on functional
descriptions
We often use natural language to describe program functionality, and generating programs
automatically from natural language descriptions is extremely challenging. The diversity of
natural language texts and programs, the ambiguity of text, and the complex structure of code
make establishing the connection between text and code a difficult problem. In this section, we
describe how code generation and completion can be performed based on functional descriptions
using the tools NL2SQL and NL2IFTTT.

chunks.heading: NL2SQL
chunks.content:
NL2SQL
NL2SQL (Natural Language to SQL) is a cutting-edge research direction in conversational user
interfaces (Conversation User Interface, CUI), aiming to convert user input in natural language
into executable SQL statements, thereby improving the efficiency of user data queries. Currently,
the main challenge hindering the value realization of big data is the high threshold for data access,
relying on database administrators to write complex SQL statements, and the added complexity
and diversity of Chinese expressions. There is substantial research in this field both domestically
and abroad, with most of the well-known NL2SQL datasets being in English, such as WikiSQL,
Spider, CoSQL, etc.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 328
A typical three-layer architecture of NL2SQL is shown in Figure 9.11.
Figure 9.11: Typical three-layer architecture of NL2SQL
NL2SQL consists of a user interaction page, a processing unit, and a database. The processing
unit is the core of the entire architecture, responsible for semantic parsing and connecting the
interaction channel between the user and the system, encompassing key technologies such as
intelligent word segmentation, entity recognition, and knowledge retrieval. In the research
direction of converting natural language into executable SQL statements, the internal algorithms
of the processing unit are gradually evolving toward deep learning.
In the Chinese NL2SQL competition, the research team from the National University of Defense
Technology proposed the M-SQL model, which achieved 92% accuracy on Chinese datasets. In
addition, running one epoch of the M-SQL model on a single 2080Ti GPU takes 20 minutes, and
the model only needs 3–4 epochs to converge.
Unlike the M-SQL model from the National University of Defense Technology, Google’s Analyza
uses a semantic parsing and rule-based approach, which offers strong controllability but requires
manual maintenance of rules. Analyza implements NL2SQL through deep learning using an
encoder-decoder architecture, recognizing several SQL clauses, including SELECT and WHERE
clauses, and sometimes involving operators such as GROUP BY and LIMIT. Each part involves
many details, such as table recognition, attribute recognition, etc. Different algorithms make
improvements and optimizations on these details within this framework to achieve better results.

Although end-to-end NL2SQL solutions can reduce manual maintenance costs, they perform
well only in simple scenarios like WikiSQL. For more complex scenarios, such as Spider or CoSQL,
accuracy is relatively low, and it is difficult to meet commercial application requirements.

chunks.heading: NL2IFTTT
chunks.content:
NL2IFTTT
IFTTT stands for ‘ if this then that ’. It is an innovative platform service that determines whether
to execute the next command based on conditions from different platforms. For example, when
someone in an IM marks a photo containing you, the photo can automatically be backed up to
your phone’s photo album. This approach meets the user’s need to link content from service A
to service B, without requiring manual intervention—the related action can be initiated and
completed automatically by IFTTT.
NL2IFTTT generates IFTTT code through natural language. Compared to commonly used
programming languages, its structure is more concise and easier to learn in terms of its structural
rules. IFTTT is based on task-triggered conditions, similar to a simplified programming language,
that is, ‘if behavior B of event A occurs, then execute C.’
Language-model-based approaches extend these earlier methods by learning statistical and
semantic patterns from large collections of code, enabling more flexible prediction, completion,
and generation.
Code generation and completion based on language models
Language models are widely used in various natural language processing tasks, such as machine
translation, speech recognition, question answering systems, etc. Language models define
the probability distribution of token sequences in natural language. Due to the naturalness
of programming languages, language models are also applied to program modeling, usually
by directly inputting parsed code snippets (at the word or character level) as text. The goal of
this model is to model the textual probability distribution of programming languages, i.e., the
probabilistic model is used to estimate the probability distribution P (s) of a code snippet s. For
a code snippet s = { w 1, …, w m }, the language model calculates the probability distribution of the
entire code snippet by computing the conditional probability of each word based on the previously

NL2IFTTT is included here as a case study in DSL-targeted code generation rather
than as a representative of mainstream NL-to-code research.

Naturalness of Software, many works utilizing N-gram models emerged subsequently. Although
N-gram can effectively learn the local context of code snippets, it cannot understand the semantic
information of code snippets. To address this problem, many researchers have improved the
N-gram model by combining the characteristics of software engineering tasks. Nguyen et al., in
the paper A Statistical Semantic Language Model for Source Code, proposed the idea that the SLAMC
model incorporates global information into the N-gram model; SLAMC combines semantic
information and models rules for semantic annotations. This method achieved a significant
improvement in the accuracy of code recommendation compared to a regular N-gram. Meanwhile,
Raychev et al., in the paper Code Completion with Statistical Language Models, also proposed
combining the N-gram model with RNN, actively suggesting appropriate API calls based on the
context during Java development to implement code completion. To address the challenge of the
locality property of code, Tu et al. proposed in the paper On the Localness of Software to introduce
a caching mechanism into the N-gram model, utilizing the characteristic that identifiers tend to
repeatedly appear within a close range, thereby achieving significant results in code prediction.
Compared to N-gram, RNN can not only capture regularities among words in a sentence, but
also detect relationships between more distant words. To further address the long-distance
dependency problem, many RNN-based variants, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and
Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), have been proposed and widely applied. As shown in Figure 9.12,
RNN models can effectively model source code and learn vector representations of source code.

The paper DeepAM-Migrate APIs with Multi-Modal Sequence to Sequence Learning focuses on using
RNN to learn vector representations that differentiate Java and C# API, and applies these learned
vectors to the API migration task between these two languages to generate code at the API level.
Many researchers have used RNN models for code token prediction and completion, achieving
remarkable results. Most research models code at the word level using RNNs, but due to the large
number of variables in code, learning becomes very challenging; therefore, some work has started
to model code at the character level.
Programming languages exhibit certain local repetitiveness. For example, a defined variable is
often reused later in the code. However, these variables are largely treated as out-of-vocabulary
(OoV) words, usually represented as UNK. Predicting a UNK is of no help to programmers in their
coding, so researchers have considered incorporating pointer network mechanisms into language
models to accurately predict locally repeated words. The pointer network can effectively copy
words that need to be reused from the input code snippet. Pointer networks were first proposed at
the 2015 IEEE conference, originally used to solve combinatorial optimization problems, and are
a variant of neural machine translation models (i.e., sequence-to-sequence models, Seq2Seq
models). In pointer networks, the attention mechanism is simpler, as it does not consider the
input elements, but instead points to them probabilistically.
In 2016, Bhoopchand et al. proposed a Sparse Pointer Network in the paper Learning Python Code
Suggestion with a Sparse Pointer Network, mainly addressing the issue of predicting custom identifiers
(such as class names, method names, variable names, etc.). The paper defines the concept of
“memory” to store the previous K identifiers. The method maintains a vector m=[id1,...,id*K*],
used to record the positions of identifiers in the global vocabulary, i.e., pointers to the global
vocabulary.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 332
At each prediction step, the network combines the global language model distribution, the pointer
probability distribution over custom identifiers, and the current code input to determine the output
word. Compared to traditional recurrent neural networks (without the attention mechanism),
this method increases the accuracy for predicting custom Python identifiers by about 25%.
In their 2018 paper Code Completion with Neural Attention and Pointer Networks, Li et al. proposed
a method for code completion by combining a language model with an attention mechanism
and pointer networks, modeling sequences of abstract syntax trees (ASTs). This model can not
only predict the type of AST nodes but also predict their values, that is, the code to be completed.

When predicting code, the entropy of parent nodes is greater than that of child nodes, resulting
in higher prediction accuracy. Therefore, their attention mechanism incorporates the parent-
child node relationship of syntax trees into the traditional attention mechanism. The paper uses
pointer networks to copy words from the input code snippets to predict OoV tokens. By defining
a selector, the model decides whether to predict the next word based on the distribution over
the global vocabulary in the language model or to use the pointer network to copy a word from
the input code snippet. This method was validated on both Python and JavaScript datasets, and
results show that the method performs exceptionally well in OoV prediction scenarios.
Although code generation and completion technologies have advanced significantly, they still
face practical limitations when applied to real software projects. The next section examines the
main issues that affect their reliability, adaptability, and usefulness in production development
environments.
Identifying pain points in code generation and
completion
Overall, code generation and completion based on LLM technology has become a trend, but the
application of this technology is still at an early stage, mainly facing the following pain points.
Uneven quality of training corpora
In daily work, the corpora used to train models can be roughly divided into two categories: one
consists of programs constructed artificially based on DSL technology, and the other consists of
project programs crawled from open source communities. Programs based on DSL usually have
relatively simple syntax and short length, making them easy to train and test; however, models
designed for DSL are difficult to generalize to other languages. Project programs crawled from
open source communities are closer to actual software development, but it is difficult to guarantee
the quality of the code.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 333
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 333
Low-quality, non-standard code introduces additional noise risk to neural networks, and code
that uses different programming conventions causes confusion for neural network models during
training and prediction. Therefore, how to obtain a unified, standardized, high-quality program
corpus is a challenge.
Weak generalization ability of program code
Much program code consists of business domain-specific logic, requiring a substantial amount
of domain-specific logic resources and a deep understanding of the various services relied on by
existing businesses. New businesses need to train their own models based on their own material
libraries, and the services required by completely new businesses often need to be developed
from scratch. Supplying new materials can also be difficult, unless all the dependent services are
indivisible atomic services; thus, making the logic model universal is hard to achieve.
Information asymmetry between functional descriptions and
program code
In actual project development, it is common for requirement descriptions to be more advanced
and abstract than functional descriptions. Requirement descriptions must first be converted
into functional descriptions, then into code descriptions, and finally, program code is generated.
At each stage, there will be information loss, which is currently typically compensated for by
programmers’ business knowledge and programming experience. There are three solutions for
directly generating code from functional descriptions:
• End-to-end generation of abstract syntax trees from requirement descriptions. If the
product definition’s description of software functionality is precise enough, this is
equivalent to creating a higher-level descriptive language
• Abstracting and encapsulating the entire chain from functional description to code as
a larger-grain functional description. Most encapsulation-based methods are currently
feasible and effective, with a typical example being NL2IFTTT.
• Developers deeply engage in each business domain, and at each stage, from functional
description to code, the model understands layer by layer and gradually generates the code
Therefore, the quality of the corpus and the accuracy of the model are crucial.
The limitations of code generation and completion become more pronounced when models are
asked to work across real project repositories rather than isolated functions or snippets. This is
where agent-based methods become important: they combine code LLMs with tools, execution
environments, documentation, and iterative feedback to support more complex project-level
development tasks.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 334
Applying agent-based methods to project-level code
generation
Agent-based project-level code generation extends single-function code completion by combining

chunks.content:
a code LLM with tools — a code execution sandbox, a static analyzer, a documentation lookup
— orchestrated by an LLM agent that plans, calls tools, and iterates. The Xcoder team at Peking
University has achieved significant results in research on the application of code LLM-based
agents in the field of software engineering, publishing several relevant papers. Xcoder is an early
example of a code LLM-based agent system that combines a code-focused language model with
tools to address project-level code generation problems. This section uses Peking University’s
paper CODEAGENT—Enhancing Code Generation with Tool-Integrated Agent Systems for Real-World
Repo-level Coding Challenges to explain Agent-based project-level code generation methods.
Pain points of project-level code generation in enterprises
Project-level code in enterprises, as a critical component supporting and driving the core business
processes, is directly related to the quality of the enterprise’s products and services, operational
efficiency, and market competitiveness. However, project-level code often involves diverse library
and function calls, complex contextual dependencies across the codebase, and various types of
code documentation. Furthermore, as business requirements change, the project code needs
constant updating, expansion, and optimization. In this dynamic, ongoing, and complex process,
there are numerous pain points.
Difficulty in fine-grained code modification and expansion
A project usually contains thousands or even tens of thousands of lines of code, involving multiple
interdependent modules and subsystems. When faced with the need for fine-grained code changes,
even a “single move can affect the whole picture”; a slight mishap can impact other modules,
leading to extensive testing and verification work. This further affects project schedules and
increases the complexity and risks of maintenance.
Complex and large codebases
Large-scale projects generally have long cycles and high staff turnover. The complexity and
vastness of the codebase make it difficult for new team members to quickly grasp the project
structure and code logic; even experienced members face time-consuming and labor-intensive
efforts when searching for specific code fragments in the ever-growing codebase.

Difficulty ensuring code generation quality
In actual programming, developers commonly use various tools to assist with coding, such as
search engines, documentation readers, and code testing tools. Although code LLMs possess
powerful code generation capabilities, they lack the ability to interact with these tools, which
limits their performance in complex tasks. Moreover, due to issues such as hallucinations with
code LLMs, the generated code may use incorrect APIs, making it difficult to ensure the quality
and reliability of code generation.
Low efficiency in implementing requirements into code
Throughout the entire project development process, enterprises often face issues such as
insufficient requirement understanding, frequent architecture design adjustments, difficulty
controlling development progress, and inadequate test coverage. These result in low iteration
efficiency, project delays, budget overruns, or substandard quality, further increasing operational
burdens and impacting market competitiveness.
Facing numerous pain points and challenges in project-level code generation, introducing
Agents has become a key path for enterprises to resolve difficulties in code generation, improve
development efficiency and code quality, and accelerate product iteration.
Technical implementation of agents
The technical implementation of a code agent can be understood from two related perspectives:
how the agent is evaluated in realistic repository-level tasks, and how the agent uses tools to
navigate code, gather context, generate implementations, and test the results. The following
discussion first examines the testing process used to evaluate Code Agent, then explains the
framework and tool integration that support project-level code generation.
Code agent testing process
The Xcoder team at Peking University conducted extensive testing on the Code Agent. Since
enterprises mainly use open-source codebases in actual coding processes—and codebases contain
a large number of complex code invocation relationships—testing within a codebase is the only
way to obtain precise results, enabling the code LLM agent to function properly. To this end,
the team configured corresponding corpora for each test task, including documentation, code
dependencies, and runtime environment.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 336
Documentation is the main input for testing and mainly describes the target for corpus generation.
The documentation provides information beyond natural language requirements, including class-
level (class names, signatures, and member functions) and function-level (function descriptions
and parameter descriptions) information. Generally, the correctness of programs generated by the
Agent can be verified by testing tools. The generated program must meet interface requirements

(e.g., input parameters), so the documentation under test also provides the type and explanation
for input parameters and output values. Considering that requirements often involve terms specific
to certain domains, the documentation also explains these terms, such as certain mathematical
formulas. Related test information is shown in Figure 9.13.
Figure 9.13: Test information for generated programs
The team specifically tested for context dependencies, which is a distinct feature from the
experiments of others. From the perspective of code generation and completion, this testing detail
is especially important because, in actual applications, a class or function usually interacts with
other code fragments in the same codebase. Such situations often occur in import statements
or within the same project, where user-defined code also depends on other user-defined code.
The interactions and dependencies among these codes can happen within the same file or span
multiple files.

For example, implementing the RandomForest class in Figure 9.14 depends on the boot-strap_
sample function in rf.py and the DecisionTree class in dt.py. This is a case of complex code
context dependency.
Figure 9.14: Contextual dependency of code
During the testing process, the tool designed by the Xcoder team at Peking University extracts
all user-defined elements (such as class names, function names, constants, and global variables)
as well as public library names from each file and stores these elements in a knowledge base. For
any defined function, the tool can use the knowledge base to locate its source file, parse the file
to identify all user-defined symbols and public libraries, and finally determine their contextual
dependencies through exact matching of symbol names and scopes.
During testing, the Xcoder team found that each example averaged about 3.1 code dependencies,
which is very similar to programming conditions in real-world projects. Since there are certain
differences between the test runtime environment and natural language in reality, the main
validation method is to determine whether the programming language generated by the code
LLM can be executed correctly and successfully return the target result. Usually, developers wait
for execution feedback and constantly correct errors in the program. In this Code Agent test, the
Xcoder team built a sandbox environment for each task. The sandbox environment provides all
the configuration needed to run the repository and offers a concise way of interaction to ensure
comprehensive testing.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 338
Technical implementation of code agent
The Xcoder team from Peking University conducted a preliminary exploration of evaluating and
enhancing the capabilities of code LLMs in repository-level code generation. Referring to the paper
Toward a Unified Agent with Foundation Models, the team proposed a new code-agent framework
based on code LLMs: Code Agent. This framework leverages external tools to enhance the code
LLM’s ability to solve problems in complex repository-level code generation. Whenever tools
are called, the Code Agent seamlessly and automatically generates code and outputs the results
after integration. Code Agent can help code LLMs complete the entire automatic code generation
process, including information gathering, code implementation, and code testing, and interact
better with software coding tools, as shown in Figure 9.15.
Figure 9.15: The process of automatic code generation
The core of Code Agent is the code navigation tool, which is used to quickly locate relevant code
items in the codebase (i.e., predefined symbol names and code snippets). Code LLMs can quickly
obtain these code items and integrate them into the code generation process. This approach can

The code navigation tool is implemented based on tree-sitter technology. Taking Python as an
example, a code navigation tool is built for the Python codebase. This tool parses and retrieves
code items in two ways. One way is to perform static analysis on files or modules and provide the
symbol names defined within, including global variables, function names, and class names. The
other way is to navigate public classes or function symbols and define separate class names or
function names for them. By combining these two methods, the code navigation tool can quickly
traverse the predefined source code in the repository, enabling code LLMs to understand complex
dependencies in the code and utilize them swiftly.
After introducing the Code Agent framework, the discussion now turns to practical development
scenarios where agent-based coding assistance can be applied in real project workflows.
Application of transaction automation in development
scenarios
In large-scale, complex projects, as users continually raise new requirements and features are
iteratively updated, developers often receive tasks to modify and extend numerous details in
large codebases, such as bug fixes, feature development, or performance optimization. aiXcoder’s
transaction automation feature can accurately parse complex transactions submitted by developers,
automatically locate problems and requirements, fully leveraging the codebase’s various modules,
interdependencies, and contextual information to process issues and requirements step-by-
step. Ultimately, it directly generates code files and autonomously creates a sandbox to validate
the edited code. During this process, it supports modifications across multiple files and can be
interrupted at any time for manual intervention and adjustments.
The following examples use aiXcoder to illustrate how agent-based coding capabil -
ities can appear in developer-facing tools, but the same general pattern can apply
to other code agents that combine models, repository context, execution feedback,
and development tools.

Figure 9.16: Information management system development scenario
The developer requests to add student-related information in two separate files and requires
that the system run properly. The transaction automation feature understands and analyzes the
request, plans, and locates the corresponding files. Notably, during automatic execution, it also

them together, and, after verification with no issues, finally generates the code files as required.
The transaction automation function not only reduces the amount of time developers spend on

Project R&D Q&A scenarios
Through the codebase Q&A feature, developers can ask questions using natural language to
achieve real-time interaction with the codebase, addressing key issues such as code architecture,
implementation logic, code dependencies, and calling relationships. This enables quick access to
and understanding of the knowledge and best practices within the enterprise codebase, thereby
accelerating the development process and improving code consistency and quality. Meanwhile, the
system will automatically predict the next question based on historical queries, further optimizing
the developer’s learning path and work efficiency.

quickly understand the project progress and master the codebase by asking questions such as:
how the modules are dependent on each other, what submodules are in a specific folder, detailed
explanations of a certain module, what a particular class is defined as and its purpose, and so on,

From requirements to complete project-level code
generation scenarios
aiXcoder’s end-to-end code generation feature supports the direct transformation of natural
language requirements provided by Product Managers or Designers into precise code, covering
requirement analysis, system design, project management, development, testing, and other stages,
generating complete project-level code and related documentation.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 342
During the AI code generation process, developers can modify and adjust intermediate deliverables
(such as requirement documents, partial code modules, test cases, etc.) to ensure they meet specific
requirements and standards. At the same time, enterprises can customize the R&D process and
the content of intermediate deliverables according to their own needs. Enterprises can specify
particular coding standards, design patterns, or testing standards, and require the AI to generate
corresponding documents and code based on these specifications.
This feature provides a more efficient collaboration mechanism for software development. For a
simple example, Agents are assigned different roles: Product Manager, Project Manager, Architect,
R&D Engineer, and Test Engineer. It can understand user requirements, perform interactive and
immersive programming, plan step by step, collaborate across multiple roles, call commonly
used development tools, provide real-time progress feedback, verify results, improve outputs,
and ultimately complete the code generation task, as shown in Figure 9.18.

The end-to-end code generation feature covers the complete R&D process, achieving full-process
automation from requirements analysis to coding, enabling quick response to user needs and
feedback, significantly improving development efficiency, shortening the time from concept to
product launch, and enhancing the product’s market competitiveness. At the same time, it reduces

Summary

As a core aspect of project management, requirements analysis plays a critical role that cannot

its intended goals. In traditional project management, requirements analysis is the process of
identifying and understanding what the client or user needs. This step is crucial to ensuring the
ultimate success of the project. Traditional methods of requirements analysis include meetings,
individual interviews, focus groups, surveys, and questionnaires. These methods have many

These pain points usually arise because traditional requirements analysis depends heavily on

• Traditional requirements analysis is time-consuming and inefficient. Organizing and
conducting physical meetings often requires coordinating the schedules of numerous
participants, which is a complex and time-consuming task in itself. Additionally, the
information collected from meetings may need further organization and analysis before
useful conclusions can be drawn. Moreover, user interviews and questionnaire surveys
typically require significant manpower to carry out—from designing questionnaires to
distributing, collecting, and analyzing the data—each step consumes a great deal of time,

• Limited by participants’ experience and cognitive biases. Requirements analysis often

their own experience and preferences, neglecting or misunderstanding the user’s real
intentions and needs. In addition, due to differences in cultural background, language
communication, or personal preferences, users may not express their needs precisely,
which can easily lead to misinterpretations or omissions of information.

• There is a quality balance issue in requirements analysis. In traditional requirements

quantity, the depth and accuracy of data may be sacrificed, and balancing these two
aspects is always difficult.

When applied to requirements analysis, LLMs help address limitations in several practical ways:
• Rapid Processing of Large Amounts of Data: LLMs can efficiently process massive text
datasets, such as lengthy project files, intensive email correspondence, and detailed
meeting minutes. Analyzing this content manually could require significant time and
effort, while LLMs can accomplish the same tasks quickly, saving vast resources.
• Deep Learning and Understanding: Leveraging advanced machine learning algorithms
and extensive training datasets, LLMs can not only identify keywords and phrases in text
but also understand their context and underlying meaning, providing more accurate
information extraction and content analysis.
• Uncovering Implicit Requirements: In traditional requirements analysis, some latent
but unexpressed needs can easily be overlooked. LLMs can use contextual reasoning and
pattern recognition to discover these implicit requirements, helping project teams grasp
a more comprehensive picture of needs.
• Adaptation to Multiple Text Formats: Whether it’s structured reports, unstructured social
media posts, or ad hoc meeting notes, LLMs can comprehend and process different text
formats and extract valid information from these diverse data sources.
• Cross-Domain Knowledge Integration: Cross-domain requirements analysis is often
limited by the analyst’s knowledge scope. Since LLMs are trained on texts covering a wide
range of topics, they possess cross-industry and cross-domain knowledge bases, enabling
them to take richer background knowledge into account and provide comprehensive
insights during analysis.
• Continuous Learning and Improvement: With ongoing input of new data, LLMs can
continue learning and adapting to new linguistic environments and requirement changes,
keeping their analytical abilities up to date.
• Unbiased Objective Analysis: Unlike human analysts who may have cognitive biases,
LLMs can perform unbiased data analysis, objectively distilling information to ensure
the accuracy and fairness of requirements analysis.
• Decision Support: By providing accurate requirements analysis, LLMs can assist managers
and decision-makers in better understanding market and user needs, optimizing the
decision-making process, and thereby improving the success rate and efficiency of projects.

more adaptable understanding of project requirements.

Effective communication gives project teams better visibility into their work, but visibility alone

Managing project risks and supporting decisions
Project risk management is a key part of the project management process, involving the
identification, assessment, monitoring, and response to uncertainties and potential threats that
may arise in the project.
• Risk Identification: At each stage of the project, the team needs to identify internal and
external factors that may affect project outcomes. This includes technical issues, resource
shortages, policy changes, etc.
• Risk Assessment: This step involves assessing the likelihood and potential impact of
each risk. It is usually achieved through qualitative and quantitative methods, such as
risk matrices or simulations.
• Risk Monitoring: Regularly monitor identified risks and adjust risk assessments based
on project progress and changes in the external environment.
• Risk Response: Develop risk response strategies, such as avoidance, mitigation, transfer,
or acceptance of risks, and integrate them into the project plan.
With the development of artificial intelligence technologies, LLMs have demonstrated great
potential in risk prediction and decision support.
In terms of risk prediction, LLMs can predict potential risks by analyzing historical data and
industry-specific trends. This kind of prediction helps team members identify possible issues
earlier and thus take preventive measures.
In terms of decision support, LLMs can provide data-driven decision support, helping project
managers evaluate possible outcomes of different response strategies. For example, AI models
can simulate the impact of different risk response measures on project timelines and costs, thus
helping management make more informed decisions.

Risk management
In project management, risk management is a strategy for identifying, assessing, and prioritizing
potential issues, aimed at reducing or avoiding their impact on the project. Effective risk
management helps the project team foresee future challenges and take measures to prevent or
resolve potential problems at the lowest cost.
Although the importance of risk management is widely acknowledged, in practice, accurately
identifying, and evaluating all possible project risks remains challenging. The complexity of
historical data, the hidden nature of bottlenecks, and anomalies in processes can all lead to delays
and incompleteness in risk management work.
The significance of risk management lies not only in reducing the impact of potential issues on
the project, but also in helping the project team anticipate future challenges and take measures
to prevent or resolve potential problems at the lowest cost. This forward-looking approach helps
the project team better cope with changes and uncertainties, thereby increasing the likelihood
of project success.
For example, risk management is like a grand outdoor wedding. The bride, groom, and planning
team must consider factors such as rain, late-arriving vendors, or any other issues that could
affect the smooth running of the wedding. By identifying these potential “risks” in advance,
they can develop contingency plans, such as preparing a tent in case it rains or confirming with
vendors ahead of time to avoid delays. This proactive risk management approach helps ensure
the wedding proceeds smoothly, just as it does in project management, helping to ensure the
successful implementation of the project. However, it is not easy to predict all possible risks.
Like trying to forecast the weather, sometimes situations can suddenly change, requiring quick
adjustments.
LLM applications employ natural language processing techniques to extract information from
project reports, change logs, meeting minutes, task statuses, and other texts, thereby predicting
potential future risk points. Combined with advanced risk monitoring and early warning systems,
projects can be monitored in real time; as soon as potential risk signals are detected, project
managers are immediately alerted and given specific improvement suggestions, making risk
management more proactive and forward-looking. LLMs are not just tools; they represent
an entirely new methodology that integrates knowledge from statistics, operations research,
cognitive psychology, and data science, among other disciplines. Through this interdisciplinary
integration, project risk management can gain a deeper understanding of how risks arise and
mitigate their impact through early intervention.

In addition, in practical applications, LLMs can be used to build risk databases, collecting and

predictions to devise preventive measures and plan response strategies in advance, thereby

LLMs provide the following three risk management approaches in project management scenarios:
predicting bottlenecks, identifying risk points, and detecting abnormal behavioral patterns.
Predicting bottlenecks
In organizations, the flow status, and the number of handovers of tasks are often hidden indicators
of project inefficiency. By using LLMs to monitor this data, potential bottlenecks can be effectively
predicted. For example, by analyzing each stage of the workflow, the model can identify key
transfer points that may cause delays. This analysis includes not only time management of tasks
but also the collaboration efficiency among team members. If the model discovers that frequent
handovers between certain teams are slowing down project progress, it can suggest optimizing
these processes. This could involve reducing unnecessary intermediate steps or introducing
automation tools to simplify the handover process, such as automatic task assignment systems
or integrated communication platforms, to improve efficiency, and transparency.
Identifying risk points
LLMs can identify potential risk points by comprehensively analyzing various project indicators
(such as task retention time, priority, deadlines, assignees’ workload, and the overall project
objectives). This type of analysis, based on historical data and predictive models, enables the
model to warn about factors that may cause the project to be overdue or deviate from set goals.
For example, if a key task is delayed multiple times consecutively, the LLM can alert the project
manager to intervene early—adjusting resources or optimizing workflows to avoid affecting the
overall project schedule.
Detecting abnormal behavior patterns
When project teams face high pressure and tight deadlines, they may exhibit irrational
behavioral patterns. With the help of cognitive psychology theories, we can better understand
the psychological mechanisms behind these behaviors. Applying these theories in the training
of LLMs can help more precisely identify such abnormal behavioral patterns. This not only helps
project managers intervene effectively during management but also allows for the establishment
of a more humane work environment and stress management systems, preventing the occurrence
of such behaviors in advance.

Once risks have been identified, the next challenge is deciding how to respond. This is where
LLMs move from detecting warning signs to helping project managers compare options, evaluate
trade-offs, and choose a course of action.
Decision support
Project decision-making is a core activity in project management. It refers to the process of
analyzing and assessing information to select the best course of action. Good decisions can
effectively promote smooth project progress and guide the project team to avoid risks at critical
moments.
In practice, project managers often face challenges such as insufficient information, time
constraints, and complex environments when making decisions. These factors increase uncertainty
in decision-making, which may lead to inaccurate or untimely decisions, thereby affecting project
outcomes.
By mining the dispersed information in the system and conducting inductive analysis, LLMs assist
project managers in reducing decision-making uncertainty. Leveraging NLP technology, LLMs
can handle complex queries and provide insights and recommendations based on data, thereby
optimizing decision quality. Decision Support Systems (DSS) integrated with LLMs can help
project managers make more informed decisions at each stage of a project. DSS can integrate
expert systems, using industry best practices and experiential rules to guide the decision-making
process. In addition, DSS can provide dynamic risk assessments and response strategies by real-
time monitoring of project metrics and changes in the external environment.
In terms of decision support, LLMs act as personal assistants for project managers, helping them
make better decisions by gathering and analyzing various types of information. Just like navigation
software recommends the best route based on current traffic conditions, LLMs can also help project
managers make decisions based on real-time project status and market conditions.
Furthermore, when project managers are overwhelmed by massive reports and emails, LLMs
can quickly filter important information and provide concise summaries, ensuring that decision-
makers don’t miss critical information—like an intelligent email sorter that helps place important
emails in the most prominent location.

During the project execution phase, teams often face uncertainties in workflows and challenges
in resource allocation. Handling complex progress reports, communication records, and resource
usage requires precise analysis and effective management, while also needing to quickly identify
and resolve bottlenecks and inefficiencies in the project. For example, a construction site may
require urgent adjustment of work arrangements due to weather changes or delays in material
delivery. This demands that project managers make rapid decisions and reallocate human and
material resources, much like a helmsman stabilizing the ship’s course in a storm.
In addition, predicting peaks and valleys in resource usage for rational allocation and determining
the most effective working models to adapt to change are also key to improving resource utilization
and productivity. Efficient problem tracking and resolution is also a challenging aspect in project
management, especially as maintaining task lists and tracking issue statuses can lead to human
errors. For larger teams, problem management becomes even more complex, creating an urgent
need to simplify issue resolution processes and quickly respond to customer feedback in order
to maintain customer satisfaction. Meanwhile, efficient and accurate search functions and issue

particularly in scaling integrated support and improving issue detection accuracy.

propose workflow optimization schemes. This is similar to how a swimming coach analyzes an

task allocation and collaboration processes. In this way, LLMs not only improve work efficiency

collaboration methods. These suggestions act like the project team’s navigation system, offering

proceeds as planned. In this way, LLMs not only help teams identify and solve current problems
but also prevent potential risks and delays, enhancing the transparency and efficiency of project
management. This data-driven, deep analysis and decision-support tool enables project teams
to maintain flexibility and responsiveness in a dynamically changing work environment, thus
achieving a higher project success rate.
Beyond recommending improvements, LLMs can also reduce manual effort by automating routine
execution tasks and generating supporting project artifacts.

to a variety of cybersecurity transformation scenarios. In security contexts, LLM technology,
with its powerful data processing capabilities and deep learning algorithms, can enhance

Reframing cybersecurity with LLMs
As LLMs become part of cybersecurity workflows, their role extends beyond improving individual
tools or automating isolated tasks. They change how security teams detect threats, interpret
large volumes of operational data, respond to incidents, and think about future risk. This shift is
especially important because modern cyber threats are no longer limited to known attack patterns;
they evolve quickly, exploit complex systems, and often require faster analysis than traditional
methods can provide. Understanding this shift requires looking at both sides of LLM adoption: the
advantages they bring to security operations and the new risks and responsibilities they introduce.
Applying LLMs in Cybersecurity 384
Advantages of LLMs in the field of security
Amid the wave of digital transformation, LLM technology is not only a new productive force in
the cybersecurity field, but also a powerful catalyst driving a new security paradigm. With the
continuous advancement of technology, LLMs are leading us into a brand-new era of cybersecurity.
In this era, traditional defense mechanisms are gradually merging with intelligent and automated
security solutions, thus forming a completely new model of security protection.
The core advantage of LLM technology lies in its ability to process massive amounts of data and
recognize complex patterns. In the field of network security, this means it can identify abnormal
behaviors from regular network traffic, predict potential attacks, and enable automated responses
to security incidents. This new paradigm is no longer solely dependent on defending against
known threats, but instead predicts and defends against unknown threats by continuously
learning behavioral patterns within networks. For example, by analyzing historical security
incidents and current network behaviors, LLMs can predict the subsequent actions of attackers
and proactively deploy defensive measures.
In addition, LLMs can play a key role in security operations. They can automate complex security
analysis tasks, freeing security analysts from tedious work and allowing them to focus on more

complex and strategic issues. This increase in efficiency enables security teams to respond more
rapidly to security events, reducing the impact of security threats on enterprise operations.
At the same time, the qualities that make LLMs useful in cybersecurity—their ability to process
large datasets, generate responses, and infer patterns from complex signals—also introduce
new concerns. Their effectiveness depends on access to reliable data, careful governance, and
safeguards that prevent the technology from being misused or trusted beyond its limits.
Challenges of LLMs in the field of security
The development of LLM technology has also brought new challenges. As the complexity of
models continues to increase, the demand for data is also growing day by day. How to efficiently
utilize data resources while ensuring personal privacy has become a key issue that needs urgent
resolution. At the same time, the decision-making processes of LLMs often lack transparency,
which poses severe challenges to the interpretability and trustworthiness of these models.
Furthermore, the powerful functions of LLMs may be misused for improper purposes, such as
generating false information for phishing or using deep learning techniques to circumvent existing
security protections.

Responding to challenges of LLM technologies
Facing the challenges brought by LLM technology, it requires coordinated efforts from the
government, enterprises, research institutions, and the public. The government should formulate
corresponding policies and regulations to standardize the application of LLM technology and
safeguard data security and personal privacy. Enterprises need to strengthen research and
development work to enhance the security and reliability of LLMs. Research institutions should
carry out in-depth studies on LLM technology and explore safer algorithms and models. The public
should also enhance their cybersecurity awareness to jointly maintain the security of cyberspace.
Looking to the future, the application of LLM technology in the field of cybersecurity has broad
prospects but is also full of challenges. Through the concerted efforts of all parties, we hope to
achieve the sound development of LLM technology. With intelligent and automated security
solutions, we can more effectively resist complex cyber threats.
While innovating technologically, we must also be alert to the security risks that LLM technology
may bring, focus on data security and privacy protection, as well as model transparency and
interpretability, and continually explore and improve response strategies to ensure the sustainable
development of the cybersecurity industry. In this contest between technology and security, only
through continuous innovation and collaboration can we harness the formidable power of LLMs
and safeguard our digital world.
This broader shift becomes clearer when viewed through the day-to-day work of security teams.
The value of LLMs is not limited to abstract improvements in intelligence or automation; it appears
in specific workflows where teams must detect unusual behavior, classify threats, investigate
incidents, prevent data leakage, and maintain compliance. The following examples show how
LLMs can support these activities across different parts of the security lifecycle.
Applying LLMs across security workflows
The impact of LLMs becomes easier to understand when it is viewed through the everyday
responsibilities of security teams. Security work involves detecting unusual behavior, classifying
threats, investigating incidents, preventing data loss, strengthening policies, training users, and
maintaining compliance across changing environments. LLMs can support many of these activities
by analyzing large volumes of structured and unstructured data, identifying patterns that may
be difficult to detect manually, and helping teams respond more quickly. The following scenarios
show how these capabilities can be applied across different stages of the security workflow.
Applying LLMs in Cybersecurity 386
Anomaly detection

As a key application of LLMs in cybersecurity, anomaly detection is gradually revealing its
important role in safeguarding network environments. Relying on advanced machine learning
algorithms, LLMs can not only learn and master standard behavioral patterns in networks but
also monitor and analyze network traffic in real time to identify and provide early warnings
of behaviors that deviate from the norm. This capability is crucial for proactively discovering
potential security threats.
Taking a large financial institution as an example, the application of LLMs can extend to multiple
levels. By deeply analyzing employees’ daily network access behaviors, LLMs can accurately
identify unauthorized access attempts, which may originate from external attackers or improper
operations by internal staff.
In addition, LLMs can monitor signs of data leakage. Whether through abnormal data transfer
patterns or unusual employee access to sensitive information, these incidents can be promptly
detected and trigger alerts.
Gartner’s report emphasizes the importance of using AI behavioral models to enhance threat
detection capabilities. Traditional threat detection methods often rely on recognizing historical
attack patterns, which proves inadequate when facing emerging and unknown threats. In contrast,
AI behavioral models, by analyzing patterns of normal behavior, can identify anomalies more
flexibly and proactively, reducing dependence on historical data and thus responding more
effectively to threats that have never occurred before.
Furthermore, the advantages of LLMs in anomaly detection are also reflected in their continuous
learning and self-optimization abilities. Over time, LLMs can continuously learn and refine
information from new data, thereby improving the accuracy of anomaly detection. Their adaptive
characteristics make LLMs particularly important in dynamic network environments, enabling
them to handle new threat patterns and rapidly adjust detection strategies.
Threat identification and classification
In the field of cybersecurity, the identification and classification of threats are the cornerstone for
building an effective defense system. LLMs, leveraging the powerful capabilities of deep learning,
are gradually becoming indispensable tools in this process. By analyzing massive amounts of
network activity data, LLMs can gain insights and extract critical features that are essential for
threat detection. These features are then used to precisely classify potential threats, providing
security teams with a clearer perspective to more effectively identify and counteract cyber attacks.

For example, security operations teams can use LLMs to distinguish and identify various types of
malware attacks, including ransomware, trojans, and worms. Each of these types of malware
has its own unique behavioral patterns and attack strategies. By learning these patterns, LLMs
help security teams quickly identify the type of attack at the earliest possible moment, so that
corresponding defensive measures can be taken. This deep-learning-based classification approach
not only greatly accelerates the speed of threat response but also offers solid data support for
developing future preventive measures.
According to research, AI-enhanced threat detection systems can significantly improve the
efficiency of threat response, reducing response time by 80%. This finding further confirms the
potential application of LLMs in the cybersecurity field. When faced with constantly evolving
cyber threats, the capability of LLMs is especially crucial. Not only can they help security teams
quickly identify known threats, but they can also predict and discover new or unknown threats
by learning behavioral patterns.
Automated threat hunting
Automated threat hunting is an innovative application of LLMs in the field of cybersecurity. By
simulating the querying and analysis processes of human analysts, it significantly improves the
efficiency and accuracy of threat detection. In this process, the LLM acts as a tireless guardian,
able to monitor network activity 24/7, perform complex data analysis tasks, and thereby identify
and alert on potential security threats.
For example, if an account initiates login attempts from multiple different geographic locations
within a short period, or if there are a large number of login attempts within a very short time,
these could be signs of account compromise or brute force attacks. The LLM can quickly capture
these anomalous behaviors and promptly relay this information to the security team, helping
them quickly locate and respond to potential security incidents.
In addition, the advantage of LLMs in automated threat hunting is also reflected in their ability to
process and analyze massive volumes of network data. In today’s network environment, enormous
amounts of data are generated every moment, which presents a huge challenge for traditional
manual analysis methods. However, with their powerful data processing capabilities, LLMs can
handle and analyze this data in a short time, greatly improving both the speed and scope of
threat detection.

Phishing attack identification
Phishing attacks, as a long-standing challenge in the field of cybersecurity, continues to
grow in complexity and stealth, presenting serious challenges to both individual users and
enterprise security. With the advancement of artificial intelligence technology, LLMs have shown

language processing technology, LLMs can analyze email contents and phishing webpages in
depth, accurately identifying fraudulent links and suspicious communication patterns, thereby
establishing a robust line of defense for cybersecurity.
Taking enterprise email systems as an example, systems integrated with LLMs can automatically
scan inbox messages, intelligently recognizing, and intercepting potential phishing emails
through learning normal communication patterns and the characteristics of phishing emails.
This automated detection and defense mechanism not only greatly improves the efficiency of
security protection but also reduces the burden on security teams, enabling them to focus more
energy on other important security tasks.
The Verizon 2021 Data Breach Investigations Report points out that phishing attacks are one of the
main causes of data breaches. This finding further highlights the importance of phishing attack
identification in cybersecurity. The application of artificial intelligence technology, especially
with the support of LLMs, is changing the traditional methods of phishing attack defense.
Through machine learning and deep learning algorithms, LLMs can learn the patterns of phishing
attacks from massive datasets and continuously optimize their identification capability, thereby
identifying and blocking these attacks in a timely manner.
Malware detection
For a long time, malware has been a major threat in the field of cybersecurity. It infiltrates systems
quietly and carries out a variety of malicious activities, including data theft, denial-of-service
attacks, and even the sabotage of critical infrastructure. To effectively counter this threat, LLM
technologies have emerged as a new tool for security defense.
LLMs use advanced machine learning and deep learning algorithms to analyze and learn
behavioral patterns and code characteristics of malware, enabling efficient detection of new or
variant malware.

By continuously analyzing file transfer behaviors, LLMs can identify files carrying malware, even
if these files have not yet been recognized by traditional virus detection systems. This is because
LLMs not only recognize known malware features, but can also detect novel or variant malware
through behavioral analysis that has not yet been widely documented.
This behavior-based detection method enables security teams to respond to potential threats
more rapidly, isolating, and removing malware in time, thus protecting user data security and
the reputation of organizations. Furthermore, this capability of LLMs is crucial in addressing
rapidly evolving malware threats. As cyber attackers continually develop new malware variants
to evade traditional detection methods, the predictive, and adaptive nature of LLMs is particularly
important today.
Intrusion detection system
The Intrusion Detection System (IDS) is an important component of the network security defense
system. Its main task is to monitor and analyze network or system behavior in order to discover
and respond to potential security threats in a timely manner. As network attack methods continue
to evolve and become more sophisticated, traditional IDSs are facing increasing challenges.
Against this backdrop, the application of LLM technology has brought new vitality and stronger
detection capabilities to IDS. With their powerful data processing and machine learning abilities,
LLMs can deeply analyze network traffic and system logs to identify various potential intrusion
behaviors. Whether it is port scanning, denial of service (DoS) attacks, or distributed denial of
service (DDoS) attacks, LLMs can improve detection accuracy and response speed by learning
the characteristics of these attack patterns.
Take a cloud service provider as an example. Such a provider may face continuous attack threats
from around the world. In this case, LLMs can be deployed at the network edge to analyze incoming
packets in real time, using their advanced algorithms to quickly identify abnormal traffic. This
allows attacks to be blocked in their early stages. This LLM-based IDS can not only improve
detection accuracy and reduce false positives and missed detections, but also achieve effective
protection for large-scale network infrastructure without affecting network performance.
LLMs in IDS also possess self-learning and self-optimization capabilities. Over time, these models
can continuously learn from new data and automatically adjust their detection strategies to adapt
to the ever-changing network environment and attack methods. This adaptive characteristic
enables LLM-based IDSs to consistently maintain efficiency and accuracy, providing a dynamic
line of defense for network security.

Security policy recommendations
In the field of network security, the application of LLMs is becoming increasingly diverse and
in-depth. They are not just tools for detecting and defending against threats, but also serve
as intelligent advisors providing strategic security recommendations. By conducting in-depth
analysis of historical security incidents and real-time monitoring of current network activities,
LLMs can offer enterprises customized security strategy advice, helping organizations build a
stronger security defense line.
Take a large enterprise as an example; its security team faces the challenge of formulating
appropriate security policies for different departments and business units in an ever-changing
network environment. LLMs play a crucial role in this process. By analyzing security vulnerabilities
and attack patterns the enterprise has encountered in the past, they can identify potential security
weaknesses and propose specific security measures accordingly. These measures may include, but
are not limited to, strong password requirements, multi-factor authentication, network access
restrictions during specific time periods, etc. Each measure is tailored to the company’s unique
needs and risk exposures. Strong password requirements can significantly enhance account
security, preventing brute-force and password-guessing attacks. Multi-factor authentication
adds an extra layer of protection to account security, making it difficult for attackers to gain full
control of accounts even if passwords are compromised. Network access restrictions during
specific time periods can effectively reduce unauthorized access during non-working hours,
thereby lowering the risk of data breaches and insider threats.
In addition, LLMs can also provide dynamic security policy recommendations based on the
results of current network activity analysis. For example, if an LLM detects an abnormal increase
in network access activity for a particular department during a specific time period, it may
recommend temporarily restricting network access for that department until the security team
completes further investigation and risk assessment.
Predictive threat modeling
Predictive threat modeling is an innovative application of LLMs in the field of cybersecurity,
representing a shift from passive defense to proactive prevention. By leveraging the powerful
computational capabilities and deep learning algorithms of LLMs, security teams are now able
to predict potential security threats and attack methods based on historical data and current
trends. This forward-looking capability greatly enhances an organization’s ability to cope with
unknown threats, enabling them to take preventive measures before an attack occurs.

In the financial industry, the application of predictive threat modeling is particularly critical. Due
to high-value transactions and sensitive data, the financial sector is a primary target for cybercrime.
By deploying LLMs, security teams can analyze vast amounts of transaction data and user behavior
patterns to identify early signs of suspicious activities. For example, LLMs can predict future
fraudulent patterns, including credit card fraud, identity theft, or money laundering activities.
Once these potential threats are identified, security teams can deploy defensive measures in
advance, such as strengthening transaction monitoring, implementing real-time fraud detection,
or adjusting risk assessment models.
The advantages of LLMs in predictive threat modeling also lie in their ability to process and analyze
unstructured data. In the field of cybersecurity, besides structured logs and transaction data, there
is a large amount of unstructured data, such as email content, social media posts, and network
traffic. LLMs, using NLP techniques, can extract valuable information from this unstructured data
and combine it with structured data to obtain more comprehensive threat predictions.
Data leakage prevention
In today’s digital era, data leakage has become one of the major security threats faced by enterprises.
LLM technology, with its outstanding data processing and analysis capabilities, is gradually
becoming an effective tool for preventing data leaks. In daily business operations, enterprises
generate a large number of log files, including network logs, system logs, application logs, and
more. These log data contain rich information but are also extremely large and complex. LLMs can
rapidly identify potential security threats through automated log analysis, such as unauthorized
access attempts, abnormal network traffic, or potential insider threats. By monitoring and
analyzing the flow of sensitive data, LLMs can effectively detect potential data leakage activities.
For example, in a certain technology company, LLMs can be trained to identify abnormal access
behaviors to sensitive information by internal personnel. Such abnormal behaviors may include
data downloads during non-working hours, unusual data transfers, or frequent access to specific
sensitive information. By learning normal data access patterns, LLMs can promptly detect activities
that deviate from the norm and notify the security team through real-time alert systems. This
real-time monitoring and rapid response mechanism is crucial for preventing data leaks.
